docs.text:
<div class="container py-4" style="max-width: 640px">
  <h1 class="h3 mb-3">Exemple 07 - la validation d'un formulaire</h1>
   <!-- novalidate: browser-specific validation is disabled, so
       afficher NOS messages, dans NOTRE style -->
  <form class="card p-4" novalidate (submit)="envoyer($event)">
    <div class="mb-3">
      <label class="form-label" for="titre">Titre</label>
      <select id="titre" class="form-select" [formField]="f.titre">
        @for (t of titres; track t) {
          <option [value]="t">{{ t }}</option>
        }
      </select>
      <div class="invalid-feedback">{{ f.titre().errors()[0]?.message }}</div>
    </div>
    <div class="row g-3 mb-3">
      <div class="col-sm-6">
        <label class="form-label" for="prenom">Prénom</label>
         <!-- the `is-invalid` class (set by configuration; see main.ts)
             encadre le champ de rouge ET fait apparaître le .invalid-feedback
             qui le suit : on y écrit la première erreur du champ -->
        <input id="prenom" class="form-control" [formField]="f.prenom">
        <div class="invalid-feedback">{{ f.prenom().errors()[0]?.message }}</div>
      </div>
      <div class="col-sm-6">
        <label class="form-label" for="nom">Nom</label>
        <input id="nom" class="form-control" [formField]="f.nom">
        <div class="invalid-feedback">{{ f.nom().errors()[0]?.message }}</div>
      </div>
    </div>
    <div class="mb-3">
      <label class="form-label" for="login">Login</label>
      <input id="login" class="form-control" autocomplete="username" [formField]="f.login">
      <div class="invalid-feedback">{{ f.login().errors()[0]?.message }}</div>
    </div>
    <div class="row g-3 mb-4">
      <div class="col-sm-6">
        <label class="form-label" for="password">Mot de passe</label>
        <input id="password" type="password" class="form-control" autocomplete="new-password" [formField]="f.password">
        <div class="invalid-feedback">{{ f.password().errors()[0]?.message }}</div>
      </div>
      <div class="col-sm-6">
        <label class="form-label" for="confirmation">Confirmation</label>
        <input id="confirmation" type="password" class="form-control" autocomplete="new-password"
               [formField]="f.confirmation">
        <div class="invalid-feedback">{{ f.confirmation().errors()[0]?.message }}</div>
      </div>
    </div>
    <button type="submit" class="btn btn-primary">Créer le compte</button>
    @if (envoiTente() && f().invalid()) {
      <div class="alert alert-danger mt-3 mb-0">Le formulaire contient {{ f().errorSummary().length }} erreur(s).</div>
    }
    @if (succes()) {
      <div class="alert alert-success mt-3 mb-0">Formulaire valide : il pourrait être envoyé au serveur.</div>
    }

  • line 5: [novalidate] disables browser-specific validation (the “Please fill in this field” tooltips): NOS messages are displayed in the NOTRE style;
  • Line 13: [f.titre().errors()]: the list of errors for the field, recalculated with each change. The message from the first one is displayed. [?.]: if there are no errors, [[0]] equals [undefined], and so does the expression;
  • Lines 21–22: the field and its message area. The class [invalid-feedback] of [Bootstrap] is hidden, unless it follows a field that has the class [is-invalid]: therefore, no code is needed to make it appear at the right time;
  • line 49: [f().invalid()]: the form is invalid if any of its fields are invalid; [f().errorSummary()] (line 50): errors for all its fields.

docs.title: 2.8. Example 08: Interactive forms
docs.text:
Before signal-based forms, [Angular] forms were written using [ngModel] (Example 05) or responsive forms ([ReactiveFormsModule]), the API being the most commonly used in existing applications. You’re bound to come across it: here is the form from Example 07, rewritten using it.

// =========================================================================
// 08-reactive-forms/src/app/app.ts - the API "history" of forms
// -------------------------------------------------------------------------
// Before signal-based forms (Angular 22), forms were written
// using FORMULAIRES RÉACTIFS (ReactiveFormsModule). These can be found in
// most existing applications: here is the form from example
// 07, rewritten using them.
//    - a FormGroup contains FormControls, one per field;
//    - each FormControl has a starting value and VALIDATEURS
//      (Validators.required, Validators.maxLength(20)...) ;
//    - in the template, [formGroup] links the <form> to the group, and
//      formControlName="name" links a HTML field to a control;
//    - the state of a control (value, errors, touched, invalid...) is a
//      ordinary property, not a signal.
// =========================================================================

import { Component, inject, signal } from '@angular/core';
import { AbstractControl, FormBuilder, ReactiveFormsModule, ValidationErrors, Validators } from '@angular/forms';

const TITRES = ['Mr', 'Mme', 'Melle'];

// A "custom" validator is applied to GROUPE: it compares two of its fields.
// It returns null (no error) or an object describing the error.
function confirmationIdentique(groupe: AbstractControl): ValidationErrors | null {
  const password = groupe.get('password')?.value;
  const confirmation = groupe.get('confirmation')?.value;
  return password === confirmation ? null : { confirmation: true };
}

@Component({
  selector: 'app-root',
  imports: [ReactiveFormsModule],
  templateUrl: './app.html',
})
export class App {
  protected readonly titres = TITRES;
  private readonly fb = inject(FormBuilder).nonNullable;

   // the group: { name: [valeur de départ, validateurs] }
  protected readonly formulaire = this.fb.group(
    {
      titre: ['Mr', [Validators.required]],
      prenom: ['', [Validators.required, Validators.maxLength(20)]],
      nom: ['', [Validators.required, Validators.maxLength(20)]],
      login: ['', [Validators.required, Validators.pattern(/^[a-z0-9._-]{1,30}$/)]],
      password: ['', [Validators.required, Validators.minLength(6)]],
      confirmation: [''],
    },
    { validators: confirmationIdentique },
  );

  protected readonly succes = signal(false);
  protected readonly valeur = signal('');

   // A field is flagged as an error if it has been modified and is invalid
  protected enErreur(nom: string): boolean {
    const controle = this.formulaire.get(nom);
    return !!controle && controle.touched && controle.invalid;
  }

   // (ngSubmit): All fields are marked as "modified," and their errors are displayed
  protected envoyer(): void {
    this.formulaire.markAllAsTouched();
    this.succes.set(this.formulaire.valid);
     // getRawValue(): the value of the entire group, typed
    this.valeur.set(JSON.stringify(this.formulaire.getRawValue()));
  }
}
  • line 18: the classes for responsive forms, in [@angular/forms];
  • lines 24–28: a “custom” validator. This is a function that takes a control (in this case, the entire group, to compare two of its fields) and returns [null] (no error) or an object describing the error;
  • line 32: the component imports [ReactiveFormsModule], which provides the directives [[formGroup]] and [formControlName];
  • line 37: [inject(FormBuilder)]: the component requests a service from [Angular] (dependency injection; see Example 14). [FormBuilder] helps generate forms; [nonNullable]: a reset field reverts to its initial value, not [null];
  • Lines 40–50: The form is a group ([FormGroup]) of controls ([FormControl]), one per field. Each is described by its initial value and the list of its validators: [Validators.required], [Validators.maxLength(20)], [Validators.pattern(...)]... Line 49: the group’s validator;
  • Lines 56–59: A field is flagged as an error if it has been modified and is invalid. The status of a check ([touched], [invalid], [errors], [value]) is a regular property, not a flag;
  • Lines 62–67: The command. [markAllAsTouched()] displays all errors; [valid] indicates whether the entire group is valid; [getRawValue()] returns its value, typed according to the group’s description.

The template:

<div class="container py-4" style="max-width: 640px">
  <h1 class="h3 mb-3">Exemple 08 - les formulaires réactifs</h1>
   <!-- [formGroup]: this <form> is controlled by the "form" group -->
  <form class="card p-4" novalidate [formGroup]="formulaire" (ngSubmit)="envoyer()">
    <div class="mb-3">
      <label class="form-label" for="titre">Titre</label>
       <!-- formControlName: this field is the "title" control of the group -->
      <select id="titre" class="form-select" formControlName="titre">
        @for (t of titres; track t) {
          <option [value]="t">{{ t }}</option>
        }
      </select>
    </div>
    <div class="row g-3 mb-3">
      <div class="col-sm-6">
        <label class="form-label" for="prenom">Prénom</label>
        <input id="prenom" class="form-control" formControlName="prenom" [class.is-invalid]="enErreur('prenom')">
         <!-- errors: an object where each key is the name of a failed validator -->
        <div class="invalid-feedback">
          @if (formulaire.controls.prenom.errors?.['required']) { Le prénom est obligatoire. }
          @if (formulaire.controls.prenom.errors?.['maxlength']) { 20 caractères au plus. }
        </div>
      </div>
      <div class="col-sm-6">
        <label class="form-label" for="nom">Nom</label>
        <input id="nom" class="form-control" formControlName="nom" [class.is-invalid]="enErreur('nom')">
        <div class="invalid-feedback">
          @if (formulaire.controls.nom.errors?.['required']) { Le nom est obligatoire. }
          @if (formulaire.controls.nom.errors?.['maxlength']) { 20 caractères au plus. }
        </div>
      </div>
    </div>
    <div class="mb-3">
      <label class="form-label" for="login">Login</label>
      <input id="login" class="form-control" formControlName="login" [class.is-invalid]="enErreur('login')">
      <div class="invalid-feedback">
        @if (formulaire.controls.login.errors?.['required']) { Le login est obligatoire. }
        @if (formulaire.controls.login.errors?.['pattern']) { Lettres minuscules non accentuées, chiffres, point, tiret, souligné. }
      </div>
    </div>
    <div class="row g-3 mb-4">
      <div class="col-sm-6">
        <label class="form-label" for="password">Mot de passe</label>
        <input id="password" type="password" class="form-control" formControlName="password"
               [class.is-invalid]="enErreur('password')">
        <div class="invalid-feedback">
          @if (formulaire.controls.password.errors?.['required']) { Le mot de passe est obligatoire. }
           <!-- The errors also contain information: the required length -->
          @if (formulaire.controls.password.errors?.['minlength']; as e) { Au moins {{ e.requiredLength }} caractères. }
        </div>
      </div>
      <div class="col-sm-6">
        <label class="form-label" for="confirmation">Confirmation</label>
         <!--: the "confirmation" error is that of GROUPE (custom validator) -->
        <input id="confirmation" type="password" class="form-control" formControlName="confirmation"
               [class.is-invalid]="formulaire.controls.confirmation.touched && formulaire.hasError('confirmation')">
        <div class="invalid-feedback">La confirmation ne correspond pas au mot de passe.</div>
      </div>
    </div>
    <button type="submit" class="btn btn-primary">Créer le compte</button>
    @if (valeur()) {
      <div class="alert mt-3 mb-0" [class]="succes() ? 'alert-success' : 'alert-danger'">
        {{ succes() ? 'Formulaire valide' : 'Formulaire invalide' }} : <code>{{ valeur() }}</code>
      </div>
    }
  </form>
</div>
  • line 4: [[formGroup]] links the form HTML to the group; [(ngSubmit)] calls the submission method;
  • line 8: [formControlName="titre"] links the field to the group’s [titre] control;
  • line 17: the class [is-invalid] is set by the template using the method [enErreur];
  • lines 20–21: [errors] is an object whose properties are named after failed validators ([required], [maxlength]...). A message is written for each possible error;
  • line 49: an error also contains information: in this case, the required length;
  • line 56: the confirmation error is that of the group: [formulaire.hasError('confirmation')].

[npm start 08-formulaires-reactifs]; a few errors, then a click on “Create Account”:

Both API perform the same function. Reactive forms describe the form in the code (controls that hold the value ET in the state), while signal-driven forms start with the data (a template to which rules are attached) and integrate naturally with the signals from the rest of the application. These are the ones we’ll use in the rest of the course and in the case study.

docs.title: 2.9. Example 09: Pipes
docs.text: A pipe formats a value for display without modifying it: [{{ valeur | pipe }}], or, with parameters, [{{ valeur | pipe: parametre1 : parametre2 }}]. [Angular] provides a dozen of them; you can write your own.

docs.title: 2.9.1. The Language of Pipes
docs.text:
Date and number pipes format values according to a language ([locale]). By default, [Angular] only supports U.S. English. For French:

import { LOCALE_ID } from '@angular/core';
import { registerLocaleData } from '@angular/common';
import localeFr from '@angular/common/locales/fr';
import { bootstrapApplication } from '@angular/platform-browser';
import { App } from './app/app';

registerLocaleData(localeFr);

bootstrapApplication(App, {
  providers: [{ provide: LOCALE_ID, useValue: 'fr-FR' }],
}).catch((erreur) => console.error(erreur));
  • line 18: [registerLocaleData(localeFr)] loads the French rules: names of days and months, decimal separator, currency symbol placement, etc.;
  • line 21: a provider that assigns a value to the token [LOCALE_ID]: the default language used by the pipes. [{ provide: jeton, useValue: valeur }] is the simplest form of a provider; Example 14 will revisit this.

docs.title: 2.9.2. Two Custom Pipes
docs.text:
A pipe is a class decorated by [@Pipe], whose method [transform] receives the value placed before the slash, along with any parameters:

// =========================================================================
// 09-pipes/src/app/pipes/horaire.pipe.ts - a "custom" pipe
// -------------------------------------------------------------------------
// A pipe is a class annotated with @Pipe, whose transform() method
// receives the value placed on the bar (and, optionally,
// parameters) and returns what should be displayed:
//      {{ time slot | time          }} -> "8:00 - 8:20"
//      {{ time slot | time: 'start' }} -> "8:00"
// A pipe is "pure" by default: Angular only calls transform() if the
// value or parameters have CHANGÉ (same object = same result).
// =========================================================================

import { Pipe, PipeTransform } from '@angular/core';

export interface Creneau {
  hdebut: number;
  mdebut: number;
  hfin: number;
  mfin: number;
}

// "8:05" rather than "8:5"
function heure(h: number, m: number): string {
  return `${h}:${String(m).padStart(2, '0')}`;
}

@Pipe({ name: 'horaire' })
export class HorairePipe implements PipeTransform {
  transform(c: Creneau, partie: 'tout' | 'debut' | 'fin' = 'tout'): string {
    switch (partie) {
      case 'debut':
        return heure(c.hdebut, c.mdebut);
      case 'fin':
        return heure(c.hfin, c.mfin);
      default:
        return `${heure(c.hdebut, c.mdebut)} - ${heure(c.hfin, c.mfin)}`;
    }
  }
}
  • line 27: the pipe’s name, the one written in the templates;
  • line 29: [transform(valeur, parametre)] returns what should be displayed. The parameter is optional (default value ['tout']): [{{ creneau | horaire }}] displays [8:00 - 8:20], [{{ creneau | horaire: 'debut' }}] displays [8:00].

A pipe is pure by default: [Angular] only calls [transform] if the value or one of the parameters has changed (a different object, a different string). This is what makes it more efficient than a component method called within the template (such as [format(...)] in Example 02), which is executed every time the component is checked.

A second pipe, which calculates initials:

// 09-pipes/src/app/pipes/initiales.pipe.ts - "Marie PELISSIER" -> "MP"
import { Pipe, PipeTransform } from '@angular/core';

@Pipe({ name: 'initiales' })
export class InitialesPipe implements PipeTransform {
  transform(nomComplet: string): string {
    return nomComplet
      .split(/\s+/)
      .filter((mot) => mot !== '')
      .map((mot) => mot[0].toUpperCase())
      .join('');
  }
}

docs.title: 2.9.3. The component and its template
docs.text:
// =========================================================================
// 09-pipes/src/app/app.ts - formatting values in a template
// -------------------------------------------------------------------------
// {{ value | pipe }} or {{ value | pipe: parameter1 : parameter2 }}:
// A PIPE transforms a value for display without modifying it. Angular
// provides a dozen of them (the @angular/common module); you can write your
// your own (see pipes/). A component imports the pipes it uses.
// =========================================================================

import { Component, signal } from '@angular/core';
import {
  CurrencyPipe,
  DatePipe,
  DecimalPipe,
  JsonPipe,
  KeyValuePipe,
  LowerCasePipe,
  PercentPipe,
  SlicePipe,
  TitleCasePipe,
  UpperCasePipe,
} from '@angular/common';
import { Creneau, HorairePipe } from './pipes/horaire.pipe';
import { InitialesPipe } from './pipes/initiales.pipe';

@Component({
  selector: 'app-root',
  imports: [
    CurrencyPipe,
    DatePipe,
    DecimalPipe,
    JsonPipe,
    KeyValuePipe,
    LowerCasePipe,
    PercentPipe,
    SlicePipe,
    TitleCasePipe,
    UpperCasePipe,
    HorairePipe,
    InitialesPipe,
  ],
  templateUrl: './app.html',
})
export class App {
  protected readonly maintenant = signal(new Date());
  protected readonly jour = '2026-10-05'; // a date in the format of the API RdvMedecins
  protected readonly prix = 1234.5;
  protected readonly taux = 0.055;
  protected readonly nom = 'marie pelissier';
  protected readonly medecin = { titre: 'Mme', prenom: 'Marie', nom: 'PELISSIER' };
  protected readonly creneaux: Creneau[] = [
    { hdebut: 8, mdebut: 0, hfin: 8, mfin: 20 },
    { hdebut: 8, mdebut: 20, hfin: 8, mfin: 40 },
    { hdebut: 14, mdebut: 5, hfin: 14, mfin: 25 },
  ];
  protected readonly langages = ['TypeScript', 'HTML', 'CSS', 'JavaScript', 'SQL'];

  protected actualiser(): void {
    this.maintenant.set(new Date());
  }
}
  • Lines 11–22 and 28–41: A component imports the pipes it uses—those from [Angular] ([@angular/common])—as its own;
  • line 46: a date in the format of API [RdvMedecins]: the [date] pipe accepts a [Date] object, a number (milliseconds), or a ISO string.
<div class="container py-4" style="max-width: 820px">
  <h1 class="h3 mb-3">Exemple 09 - les pipes</h1>
  <table class="table table-sm align-middle">
    <thead><tr><th>Dans le template</th><th>Affiché</th></tr></thead>
    <tbody>
      <tr><td><code>{{ '{{' }} maintenant() | date {{ '}}' }}</code></td><td>{{ maintenant() | date }}</td></tr>
      <tr><td><code>{{ '{{' }} maintenant() | date: 'fullDate' {{ '}}' }}</code></td><td>{{ maintenant() | date: 'fullDate' }}</td></tr>
      <tr><td><code>{{ '{{' }} maintenant() | date: 'HH:mm:ss' {{ '}}' }}</code></td><td>{{ maintenant() | date: 'HH:mm:ss' }}</td></tr>
      <tr><td><code>{{ '{{' }} jour | date: 'EEEE d MMMM y' {{ '}}' }}</code></td><td>{{ jour | date: 'EEEE d MMMM y' }}</td></tr>
      <tr><td><code>{{ '{{' }} jour | date: 'longDate' : '' : 'en-US' {{ '}}' }}</code></td><td>{{ jour | date: 'longDate' : '' : 'en-US' }}</td></tr>
      <tr><td><code>{{ '{{' }} prix | currency: 'EUR' {{ '}}' }}</code></td><td>{{ prix | currency: 'EUR' }}</td></tr>
      <tr><td><code>{{ '{{' }} prix | number: '1.0-0' {{ '}}' }}</code></td><td>{{ prix | number: '1.0-0' }}</td></tr>
      <tr><td><code>{{ '{{' }} taux | percent: '1.1-1' {{ '}}' }}</code></td><td>{{ taux | percent: '1.1-1' }}</td></tr>
      <tr><td><code>{{ '{{' }} nom | uppercase {{ '}}' }}</code></td><td>{{ nom | uppercase }}</td></tr>
      <tr><td><code>{{ '{{' }} nom | titlecase {{ '}}' }}</code></td><td>{{ nom | titlecase }}</td></tr>
      <tr><td><code>{{ '{{' }} 'RDV' | lowercase {{ '}}' }}</code></td><td>{{ 'RDV' | lowercase }}</td></tr>
      <tr><td><code>{{ '{{' }} langages | slice: 0 : 3 {{ '}}' }}</code></td><td>{{ langages | slice: 0 : 3 }}</td></tr>
      <tr><td><code>{{ '{{' }} medecin | json {{ '}}' }}</code></td><td><code>{{ medecin | json }}</code></td></tr>
       <!-- two pipes in a row: the result of the first is passed to the second -->
      <tr><td><code>{{ '{{' }} nom | titlecase | initiales {{ '}}' }}</code></td><td>{{ nom | titlecase | initiales }}</td></tr>
    </tbody>
  </table>

  <h2 class="h6">keyvalue : parcourir les propriétés d'un objet</h2>
  <ul>
    @for (p of medecin | keyvalue; track p.key) {
      <li>{{ p.key }} = {{ p.value }}</li>
    }
  </ul>

  <h2 class="h6">Un pipe maison : horaire</h2>
  <ul>
    @for (c of creneaux; track $index) {
      <li>{{ c | horaire }} (début : {{ c | horaire: 'debut' }})</li>
    }
  </ul>
  <button class="btn btn-sm btn-outline-primary" (click)="actualiser()">Actualiser l'heure</button>
</div>
  • lines 6–20: one line per pipe: the expression, followed by its result. [{{ '{{' }}] displays the characters [{{], which cannot be written as-is in a template;
    • Lines 6–10: the pipe [date], with a predefined format ([fullDate], [longDate]...) or a composite format ([EEEE d MMMM y], [HH:mm:ss]). Line 10: its second and third parameters are the time zone and the language: in this case, English, for this date only;
    • line 11: [currency], an amount in a currency;
    • line 12: [number: '1.0-0']: at least 1 digit before the decimal point, between 0 and 0 digits after: rounded to the nearest whole number;
    • line 13: [percent], a percentage;
    • lines 14–16: uppercase letters, uppercase initials, lowercase letters;
    • line 17: [slice], part of a list or string;
    • line 18: [json], an object in the format JSON (very useful for debugging);
    • line 20: two pipes in a row: the result of the first is passed to the second;
  • line 26: [keyvalue] converts an object into a list of [{ key, value }] pairs, which [@for] can iterate over;
  • line 34: our pipe [horaire], first without and then with a parameter.

[npm start 09-pipes]:

[Angular] also provides the pipe [async], which displays the latest value of an observable (see Example 19), and [i18nPlural] for plurals. [ngx-translate] provides the pipe [translate], which translates text (Example 21).

The twenty-five examples have introduced the concepts we need to write the [RdvMedecins] client:

ConceptWhere it will be used in the case studycomponents, inputs, outputs, [model()], projectionthe navigation bar, form fields, windowssignals, [computed], [effect], [linkedSignal]all pages; the calendar at the following addressforms with signals, validation, custom controlslogin, doctor and client profiles, account creation, user accountpipesformatting of dates, times, and namesservices and dependency injectionlogged-in user, messages, confirmation windowthe router and its guardspages, permissions for each role, the session to be restored after F5[ngx-translate]French and English, and the translation of server errors[HttpClient], interceptor, cookie httpOnly, proxyconnection, expired session, all communication with the serverthe API access layera file [rdvmedecins.api.ts], one method per route

The client will be the exact equivalent of the HTML application from the [NestJS] course, page by page. The difference lies elsewhere: the server no longer generates any pages; it responds in JSON, and everything related to display (pages, language, date formatting, messages) has been moved to the browser.

docs.title: 6.1. Example 21: A Bilingual Application
docs.text:
The [RdvMedecins] application is available in French and English. In the [NestJS] course, the server used to translate the pages before sending them. Now, the pages are generated in the browser: the client translates them, and switching languages no longer requires any interaction with the server.

[Angular] has its own translation system, [@angular/localize], which generates a compiled application for each language: switching languages therefore simply involves loading a different application. Instead, we’ll use the [ngx-translate] library, the most commonly used one alongside [Angular], which translates at runtime: a single click is all it takes to retranslate the entire page.

21-i18n/src/app/
├── i18n/
│   ├── fr.json          le dictionnaire français
│   ├── en.json          le dictionnaire anglais
│   ├── i18n.ts          la configuration de ngx-translate
│   └── pluriel.pipe.ts  le choix du pluriel
├── app.ts
└── app.html

The library is declared in the [package.json] file in the workspace:

"@ngx-translate/core": "^18.0.0",

docs.title: 6.1.2. The configuration
docs.text:
// =========================================================================
// 21-i18n/src/app/i18n/i18n.ts - ngx-translate configuration
// -------------------------------------------------------------------------
// ngx-translate is the most widely used translation library with
// Angular. It is provided with:
//    - a DICTIONNAIRE file per language (fr.json, en.json), where each text has a
//      CLÉ ("ACCUEIL.BONJOUR"); the parameters are written as {{name}};
//    - a CHARGEUR (TranslateLoader), which returns the dictionary for a
//      language. Ours retrieves them from the application code (by importing
//      JSON files); another might download them;
//    - the source language (the one stored in localStorage, otherwise the one
//      of the browser, otherwise French) and the fallback language.
// In the templates, {{ 'ACCUEIL.BONJOUR' | translate: { name: 'Marie' } }}
// displays the text in the language COURANTE; changing the language updates the entire
// page up to date.
//
// On the client side, this works on the same principle as the NestJS course (dictionaries
// i18n/*.json + {{t}} helper) — but the translation now takes place in
// the browser, and switching languages no longer requires any server requests.
//
// (Angular also has its own system, @angular/localize, which generates UNE
// compiled application per language: you can only switch languages
// by switching pages. ngx-translate, on the other hand, translates at runtime.)
// =========================================================================

import { Provider } from '@angular/core';
import { provideTranslateLoader, provideTranslateService, TranslateLoader, TranslationObject } from '@ngx-translate/core';
import { Observable, of } from 'rxjs';
import fr from './fr.json';
import en from './en.json';

export type Langue = 'fr' | 'en';
export const LANGUES: Langue[] = ['fr', 'en'];
export const CLE_LANGUE = 'exemple21.langue';

// the dictionary loader
class DictionnairesLoader implements TranslateLoader {
  getTranslation(langue: string): Observable<TranslationObject> {
    return of(langue === 'en' ? en : fr);
  }
}

function langueDeDepart(): Langue {
  const memorisee = localStorage.getItem(CLE_LANGUE);
  if (memorisee === 'fr' || memorisee === 'en') {
    return memorisee;
  }
  return navigator.language.startsWith('en') ? 'en' : 'fr';
}

export function provideI18n(): Provider[] {
  return provideTranslateService({
    loader: provideTranslateLoader(DictionnairesLoader),
    fallbackLang: 'fr', // If a key is missing in English, the French version is used
    lang: langueDeDepart(),
  });
}
  • Lines 29–30: The dictionaries are imported as modules; they are part of the application code. This is made possible by the [resolveJsonModule] option in the [tsconfig.json] file;
  • line 34: the key under which the selected language is stored in [localStorage] (example 20);
  • lines 37–41: the dictionary loader: [ngx-translate] calls it to retrieve a language’s dictionary in the form of an observable. Ours retrieves them from the code; another might download them from the server;
  • lines 43–49: the source language: the one the user last selected, otherwise the browser’s language, otherwise French;
  • lines 51–57: [provideTranslateService] makes the services of [ngx-translate] available throughout the application. [fallbackLang]: the language used for a key missing from the current dictionary.
// =========================================================================
// 21-i18n/src/main.ts
// -------------------------------------------------------------------------
// provideI18n(): ngx-translate (see app/i18n/i18n.ts).
// registerLocaleData(localeFr): French rules for date pipes,
// currency... (English is always available).
// =========================================================================

import { registerLocaleData } from '@angular/common';
import localeFr from '@angular/common/locales/fr';
import { bootstrapApplication } from '@angular/platform-browser';
import { App } from './app/app';
import { provideI18n } from './app/i18n/i18n';

registerLocaleData(localeFr);

bootstrapApplication(App, { providers: [provideI18n()] }).catch((erreur) => console.error(erreur));
  • line 15: the pipes [date] and [currency] (example 09) know the rules for English; those for French must be registered;
  • line 17: the services for [ngx-translate] are added to the application.

docs.title: 6.1.3. Plurals
docs.text:
[ngx-translate] does not support plurals. A small pipe selects the correct form:

// =========================================================================
// 21-i18n/src/app/i18n/pluriel.pipe.ts - choosing the plural form
// -------------------------------------------------------------------------
// ngx-translate does not support plurals. The dictionary provides the
// forms under the same key ("RENDEZ_VOUS": { "zero", "one", "other" }) and
// this pipe selects the correct one based on number and language:
//      {{ 'ACCUEIL.RENDEZ_VOUS' | plural: n : language | translate: { n } }}
// Intl.PluralRules knows the rules for each language ("one" or "other" in
// French and English, but other forms in Polish, Arabic...).
// =========================================================================

import { Pipe, PipeTransform } from '@angular/core';

@Pipe({ name: 'pluriel' })
export class PlurielPipe implements PipeTransform {
  transform(cle: string, n: number, langue: string | null): string {
    if (n === 0) {
      return `${cle}.zero`;
    }
    return `${cle}.${new Intl.PluralRules(langue ?? 'fr').select(n)}`;
  }
}
  • Lines 16–21: The pipe receives a key ([ACCUEIL.RENDEZ_VOUS]), a number, and a language; it returns the key in the correct form ([ACCUEIL.RENDEZ_VOUS.one], for example);
  • Line 18: Zero has its own format (“no appointment”);
  • line 20: [Intl.PluralRules], provided by the browser, follows the rules for each language: [one] or [other] in French and English, but other forms in Polish or Arabic. (Note: In French, 1.5 is singular; in English, it is plural.)

docs.title: 6.1.4. The translated page
docs.text:
// =========================================================================
// 21-i18n/src/app/app.ts - a translated page
// -------------------------------------------------------------------------
//    - 'CLE' | translat                   e a text;
//    - 'CLE' | translate: { name: ...      } text with parameters;
//    - date / currency in the curren      t language a date or amount in the format
//                                           of the current language;
//    - translate.use('en'                 ) changes the language: the entire
//                                           page is re-translated.
// TranslateService.currentLang is a SIGNAL: the current language.
// =========================================================================

import { Component, effect, inject, signal } from '@angular/core';
import { CurrencyPipe, DatePipe } from '@angular/common';
import { TranslatePipe, TranslateService } from '@ngx-translate/core';
import { CLE_LANGUE, Langue, LANGUES } from './i18n/i18n';
import { PlurielPipe } from './i18n/pluriel.pipe';

@Component({
  selector: 'app-root',
  imports: [CurrencyPipe, DatePipe, TranslatePipe, PlurielPipe],
  templateUrl: './app.html',
})
export class App {
  private readonly translate = inject(TranslateService);
  protected readonly langue = this.translate.currentLang;
  protected readonly langues = LANGUES;
  protected readonly nombre = signal(2);
  protected readonly aujourdhui = new Date();

   // what the RdvMedecins server would return (see the chapter on the black box)
  protected readonly reponsesServeur = [
    { statusCode: 409, cle: 'ERRORS.LOGIN_TAKEN', params: {} },
    { statusCode: 429, cle: 'ERRORS.TOO_MANY_ATTEMPTS', params: { minutes: '15' } },
  ];

   // translate.translate (key): a SIGNAL that follows the current language
  private readonly titre = this.translate.translate('APP.TITRE');

  constructor() {
     // Every time the language changes: it is stored, and the page is updated
     // the page’s lang attribute (useful for screen readers and spell-checkers)
    effect(() => {
      const langue = this.langue();
      if (langue) {
        localStorage.setItem(CLE_LANGUE, langue);
        document.documentElement.lang = langue;
      }
      document.title = String(this.titre());
    });
  }

  protected choisir(langue: Langue): void {
    this.translate.use(langue);
  }
}
  • line 21: [TranslatePipe]: the pipe [translate];
  • line 25: [TranslateService]: the main service of [ngx-translate];
  • line 26: [currentLang]: the current language, as a signal;
  • lines 32–35: two error responses, as the server would return them: a key and parameters;
  • line 38: [translate.translate(clé)] returns a signal equal to the translation of the key, which follows the current language;
  • lines 43–50: an action executed whenever the language changes: the language is stored (line 46), the page’s [lang] attribute is updated (line 47; this is used by screen readers and spell-checkers), as well as the tab title (line 49);
  • line 54: [use] changes the current language: the entire page is re-translated.
<div class="container py-4" style="max-width: 720px">
  <div class="d-flex justify-content-between align-items-center mb-3">
    <h1 class="h3 mb-0">{{ 'APP.TITRE' | translate }}</h1>
    <div class="btn-group btn-group-sm" role="group" [attr.aria-label]="'APP.LANGUE' | translate">
      @for (l of langues; track l) {
        <button class="btn" [class]="langue() === l ? 'btn-primary' : 'btn-outline-primary'" (click)="choisir(l)">
          {{ l.toUpperCase() }}
        </button>
      }
    </div>
  </div>

  <div class="card p-3 mb-3">
    <p>{{ 'ACCUEIL.BONJOUR' | translate: { nom: 'Marie' } }}</p>
     <!-- a parameter calculated by another pipe, in the current language -->
    <p>{{ 'ACCUEIL.AUJOURDHUI' | translate: { date: (aujourdhui | date: 'fullDate' : '' : langue() ?? 'fr') } }}</p>
    <p>{{ 'ACCUEIL.PRIX' | translate: { prix: (1234.5 | currency: 'EUR' : 'symbol' : '1.2-2' : langue() ?? 'fr') } }}</p>
     <!-- pluriel selects the key (zero, one, other), and translate translates it -->
    <p class="fw-bold">{{ 'ACCUEIL.RENDEZ_VOUS' | pluriel: nombre() : langue() | translate: { n: nombre() } }}</p>
    <div class="d-flex gap-2">
      <button class="btn btn-sm btn-outline-success" (click)="nombre.set(nombre() + 1)">{{ 'ACCUEIL.AJOUTER' | translate }}</button>
      <button class="btn btn-sm btn-outline-secondary" [disabled]="nombre() === 0" (click)="nombre.set(nombre() - 1)">
        {{ 'ACCUEIL.RETIRER' | translate }}
      </button>
    </div>
  </div>

  <div class="card p-3">
    <h2 class="h6">{{ 'SERVEUR.TITRE' | translate }}</h2>
    <p>{{ 'SERVEUR.EXPLICATION' | translate }}</p>
    <ul class="mb-0">
      @for (r of reponsesServeur; track r.cle) {
         <!-- the server key EST a dictionary key; `params` provides its parameters -->
        <li><code>{{ r.statusCode }} {{ r.cle }}</code><br>→ {{ r.cle | translate: r.params }}</li>
      }
    </ul>
  </div>
</div>
  • line 3: ['APP.TITRE' | translate]: the translation of the key in the current language;
  • line 6: the current language button is highlighted;
  • line 14: a parameterized text: the pipe receives an object that provides the value of each parameter;
  • lines 16–17: the value of a parameter can be calculated by another pipe. The last argument of [date] and [currency] is the language: the date and amount are written in the French or English style;
  • line 19: two chained pipes: [pluriel] selects the key, and [translate] translates it;
  • line 34: the key returned by the server is translated, along with its parameters.

docs.title: 1. Introduction
docs.text:
The document’s PDF is HERE.

The document’s codes are HERE.

This document is a product of Anthropic’s IA Claude. It follows the course “Step-by-Step Introduction to the NestJS Web Framework,” from which it shifts the perspective:

  • In the course [NestJS], the server generates the pages HTML (view engine [Handlebars]); the browser simply displays them;
  • in this course, the pages are generated in the browser by an application [Angular]; the server, now reduced to a simple server JSON, provides only data.

The application’s pages, however, remain unchanged: they are those of the [RdvMedecins] application already presented with the other frameworks (login with CAPTCHA, doctor’s schedule, appointment window, patient portal, doctor and client management, account creation, French and English).

This document follows the same structure as its predecessors: first, numerous short examples, each focusing on a specific concept from [Angular], followed by a complete case study—the [Angular] client for the [RdvMedecins] application—with all files annotated. It follows the outline of the course “Step-by-Step Introduction to the Vue.js Framework”: readers familiar with [Vue.js] will find the same examples, written in the style of [Angular]. Since [Angular] is a more feature-rich framework, there are more examples: 25 instead of 20.

A course already exists on this topic: An Example of an Angular/NestJS Client/Server (2026), which covers both the server and the client. This document differs in its approach: the server is treated as a black box, with only the API and JSON of interest to us, and we learn [Angular] step by step before tackling the full client.

docs.title: 1.1. Angular’s Role in a Web Application
docs.text:
The application has two parts, which communicate with each other only through requests:

  • 1: The [Angular] application, running in the browser, sends a HTTP request to the server, for example, [GET /api/agenda?idMedecin=1&jour=2026-10-05];
  • 2: The server responds with data JSON: this doctor’s schedule for that day. It does not generate any pages;
  • 3: Using this data, [Angular] updates the page displayed in the browser without reloading it.

The following diagram compares the two architectures:

The browser loads only a single, nearly empty page—HTML—upon startup. Everything else is generated by [JavaScript] code: this is known as a single-page application (SPA, for [Single Page Application]). When the user clicks on an internal link, no page is requested from the server: the [Angular] router changes the displayed URL and replaces the page’s content.

[Angular] is a framework created by Google. Its first version, [AngularJS] (2010), was completely rewritten in 2016: it is this rewrite, known as [TypeScript], that is now simply called [Angular], and which releases a new major version every six months. It is based on three ideas:

  • components: the interface is broken down into reusable pieces (a navigation bar, a form field, a confirmation window, etc.). A component is a [TypeScript] class, associated with a HTML template and a CSS style;
  • Responsiveness, based on signals: A component’s data is stored in signals. When one of them changes, [Angular] automatically updates the parts of the page that display it. We never write code that directly modifies the page;
  • Dependency injection: Components do not create the objects they need (server access, logged-in user, language, etc.) on their own; they request them, and [Angular] provides them. This is the mechanism that the [NestJS] course has already presented on the server side—[NestJS] was, in fact, inspired by it.

Unlike [Vue.js], [Angular] is an “all-in-one” framework: router, forms, HTTP client, animations, and tests are provided by the [Angular] team itself, along with recommended usage guidelines.

We will use [Angular] 22, with its most recent features: standalone components ([standalone]), signals, new template syntax ([@if], [@for]), signal-based forms, and change detection without [zone.js] ([zoneless]), which is the default behavior in [Angular] 22.

docs.title: 1.2. Tools Used
docs.text:
The examples were written and tested using the following tools (their installation is described in the appendix):

  • [Node.js] 24 (or at least 22.22.3: this is the requirement for [Angular] 22) and its package manager [npm];
  • the editor [Visual Studio Code], with the extension [Angular Language Service];
  • a recent browser ([Chrome], [Firefox], [Edge]), if possible with the extension [Angular DevTools];
  • the command-line tool [curl], which displays the raw HTTP responses;
  • the SGBD [MySQL] (or [MariaDB]), for example, the one from [Laragon] under [Windows]: it is required for the JSON server, as described in the chapter introducing it.

The libraries are those of the [package.json] files: [Angular] 22.2 (the core, the router, the forms, the HTTP client), the command-line tool [Angular CLI] (command [ng]), [RxJS] 7.8 (observables), [ngx-translate] 18 (languages), [TypeScript] 6.0, [Bootstrap] 5.3.

docs.title: 1.3. Examples
docs.text:
The codes in the document are organized into three folders:

livrable/
├── exemples-angular/          les 25 petits exemples d'Angular
├── rdvmedecins-nestjs-json/   le serveur JSON RdvMedecins (la « boîte noire »)
└── rdvmedecins-angular/       le client Angular de l'étude de cas

The examples folder is a workspace named [Angular] ([workspace]): it contains twenty-five small applications—one per example—that share the same libraries:

exemples-angular/
├── 01-premiere-application/
├── 02-signaux/
├── ...
├── 25-erreurs-serveur/

Install the libraries once, in a console opened to the [exemples-angular] folder (in [VS Code]: Terminal menu / New Terminal):

npm install

Then run a sample by entering its name:

npm start 01-premiere-application

The [Angular] development server compiles the example and serves it on port 4200: open it at http://localhost:4200/. This server does not need to be restarted when you modify a file: each saved file is immediately recompiled, and the browser page updates automatically. Stop it using [Ctrl-C] in the console before running the next example (only one example at a time can occupy port 4200).

Examples 22 through 25 query the server JSON [RdvMedecins]: you will need to have it installed and running, as explained in the chapter dedicated to it.

docs.title: 5.1. Example 19: Observables RxJS
docs.text:
We’ve already encountered two types of values that change over time: signals, which always have a current value, and promises, which deliver a single value at a later time. [Angular] uses a third type: observables, provided by the [RxJS] library. An observable is a stream of values that arrive over time: keystrokes, timer ticks, router events (Example 17), a server’s response (Example 22).

Their power lies in their operators: functions that transform one stream into another (filtering, waiting, discarding an expired request, etc.). This example presents the main ones in three scenarios.

// =========================================================================
// 19-rxjs/src/app/app.ts - observables from the RxJS library
// -------------------------------------------------------------------------
// A OBSERVABLE is a FLUX of values that arrive over time (the
// keyboard keystrokes, the ticking of a timer, a server's response...).
// Angular makes extensive use of them: the client HTTP (Example 22) and the router
// (Example 17) return observables.
//    - observable.subscribe (function): we subscribe to ABONNE; the function receives
//      each value. Nothing happens until someone subscribes;
//    - observable.pipe(op1, op2...): a NOUVEAU stream, transformed by
//      OPÉRATEURS (map, filter, debounceTime, switchMap...) ;
//    - toSignal (observable): a signal whose value is the last received value
//      (automatic subscription and unsubscription).
// =========================================================================

import { Component, DestroyRef, inject, signal } from '@angular/core';
import { takeUntilDestroyed, toSignal } from '@angular/core/rxjs-interop';
import { debounceTime, delay, distinctUntilChanged, filter, interval, map, Observable, of, Subject, switchMap, take, tap } from 'rxjs';

const MEDECINS = ['Marie PELISSIER', 'Paul TATOU', 'Sophie DUPONT', 'Jacques DURAND', 'Martine PELLETIER'];

@Component({
  selector: 'app-root',
  templateUrl: './app.html',
})
export class App {
  protected readonly journal = signal<string[]>([]);

   // 2. a timer: 0, 1, 2... every second; take(20): 20 values
   // then the stream ends; map: each value is transformed
  private readonly secondes$ = interval(1000).pipe(
    take(20),
    map((n) => 20 - n - 1),
  );
   // toSignal: the countdown, in the form of a signal
  protected readonly rebours = toSignal(this.secondes$, { initialValue: 20 });

   // 3. A "real-time" search: a Subject is an observable
   // in which one POUSSE generates values (next) oneself
  private readonly saisies = new Subject<string>();
  protected readonly resultats = toSignal(
    this.saisies.pipe(
      map((texte) => texte.trim().toLowerCase()),
      debounceTime(400), // we wait 400 ms without any keystrokes
      distinctUntilChanged(), // text identical to the previous one is ignored
      filter((texte) => texte.length >= 2),
      tap((texte) => this.tracer(`recherche envoyée : « ${texte} »`)),
       // switchMap: a text search; if new text arrives
       // before the response, the previous search is ABANDONNÉE
      switchMap((texte) => this.rechercher(texte)),
    ),
    { initialValue: [] as string[] },
  );

  constructor() {
     // 1. A manually created observable: it emits three values, then terminates
    const troisValeurs = new Observable<string>((abonne) => {
      abonne.next('un');
      abonne.next('deux');
      setTimeout(() => {
        abonne.next('trois (une seconde plus tard)');
        abonne.complete();
      }, 1000);
    });
     // takeUntilDestroyed: the subscription ends if the component disappears
    troisValeurs.pipe(takeUntilDestroyed(inject(DestroyRef))).subscribe({
      next: (valeur) => this.tracer(`reçu : ${valeur}`),
      complete: () => this.tracer('flux terminé'),
    });
  }

  protected saisir(texte: string): void {
    this.saisies.next(texte);
  }

   // A simulated “server”: the response arrives after a random delay
  private rechercher(texte: string): Observable<string[]> {
    const trouves = MEDECINS.filter((m) => m.toLowerCase().includes(texte));
    return of(trouves).pipe(delay(200 + Math.random() * 600));
  }

  private tracer(message: string): void {
    this.journal.update((j) => [...j, `${new Date().toLocaleTimeString()} ${message}`]);
  }
}
  • line 18: the functions and operators used are all imported from [rxjs];

A hand-built observable:

  • lines 57–64: An observable is constructed from a function, which is called for each subscriber. It emits values using [next] (lines 58, 59, 61), then signals the end of the stream using [complete] (line 62);
  • line 66: [subscribe]: the user subscribes to the stream. Nothing happens until someone subscribes: the function in lines 57–64 is executed only at that point. The object passed to [subscribe] specifies what to do with each value (line 67) and with the end of the stream (line 68);
  • line 66: [pipe] chains together operators. [takeUntilDestroyed] stops the subscription if the component disappears: a forgotten subscription would continue to run for a component that no longer exists.

A countdown:

  • Line 31: [interval(1000)] transmits 0, 1, 2... every second, indefinitely;
  • Line 32: [take(20)] keeps only the first twenty values, then terminates the stream;
  • line 33: [map] transforms each value: 0, 1, 2... become 19, 18, 17...;
  • line 36: [toSignal] converts the stream into a signal, which is set to the last received value, and which the template reads like any other signal. [toSignal] subscribes to the stream and unsubscribes when the component disappears. [initialValue]: the value of the signal before the first value in the stream.

By convention, the name of a variable that contains an observable ends with [$] (line 31).

A search as you type:

This is a classic example of observables: we want to search for doctors whose names contain the text being typed, without sending a request to the server with every keystroke, and without risking a slow response overwriting a more recent one.

  • Line 40: a ***[Subject] is an observable into which we *push values ourselves, using ***[next]***: line 73, with each keystroke (the template calls [saisir] for every [input] event);
  • line 43: the text is cleared;
  • line 44: [debounceTime(400)] only outputs a value if no other value arrives for 400 ms: as long as the user is typing, nothing is sent;
  • line 45: [distinctUntilChanged] ignores a value identical to the previous one (“pel,” then “pelx” immediately deleted: “pel” again);
  • line 46: [filter] retains only text strings of at least two letters;
  • line 47: [tap] performs an action without modifying the stream: in this case, a line in the log;
  • line 50: [switchMap] replaces each text with the result of its search (lines 77–80: a simulated server that responds after a random delay). If a new text arrives before the response, the previous search is abandoned: its response will never be displayed. With the real client HTTP, the request would even be canceled;
  • line 52: the [resultats] signal is an empty list as long as no search has been successful.
<div class="container py-4" style="max-width: 720px">
  <h1 class="h3 mb-3">Exemple 19 - les observables RxJS</h1>

  <div class="card p-3 mb-3">
    <h2 class="h6">Un compte à rebours (interval, take, map, toSignal)</h2>
    <p class="display-6 mb-0">{{ rebours() }}</p>
  </div>

  <div class="card p-3 mb-3">
    <h2 class="h6">Une recherche au fil de la frappe (debounceTime, switchMap)</h2>
    <input class="form-control mb-2" placeholder="au moins deux lettres : pel, dur..." (input)="saisir(champ.value)" #field>
    <ul class="mb-0">
      @for (r of resultats(); track r) {
        <li>{{ r }}</li>
      } @empty {
        <li class="text-muted">aucun résultat</li>
      }
    </ul>
  </div>

  <h2 class="h6">Journal</h2>
  <ol class="small">
    @for (ligne of journal(); track $index) {
      <li>{{ ligne }}</li>
    }
  </ol>
</div>
  • line 6: the countdown, a signal;
  • line 11: [#champ] is a template variable: it refers to the element [<input>], whose value is passed with each keystroke;
  • lines 13–17: the search results.

[npm start 19-rxjs]; type “pe,” then, a little later, “l”:

The log shows both searches: “pe” (sent after 400 ms of silence), then “pel.”

Signals or observables? Both coexist in [Angular], with different roles:

SignalObservableValuealways has a current value, which can be read at any timeemits values over time; no “current” valueUsagethe application's state (what is displayed)events and asynchronous operations (requests, timers, keystrokes)Subscriptionautomatic (templates, [computed], [effect])explicit ([subscribe]), or via [toSignal]Key featuresSimplicityOperators: wait, combine, abandon

The trend in [Angular] is to store the state in signals and to reserve observables for cases where their operators are useful. [toSignal] and [toObservable] alternate between the two. In the case study, the HTTP requests will be converted to promises ([firstValueFrom], Example 22), and the state will be encapsulated in signals; only router events will be listened to as observables.

docs.title: 5.2. Example 20: A Shared State
docs.text:
Several components often need the same data: the logged-in user (the navigation bar, guards, pages), messages to display, and the selected language. Where should this data be stored? The [NestJS] course addressed the same question on the server side (application, request, and session scopes). This example adapts it to the browser, with three “scopes”:

  • the local state of a component, stored in its own variables: it disappears when the component is destroyed;
  • the state of a root service: shared by all components, it survives their removal but not a page reload (F5), which restarts the application;
  • the state stored in the browser’s localStorage: it survives a page reload and even the closure of the browser.
20-etat-partage/src/app/
├── etat/
│   ├── panier.service.ts        un état partagé
│   └── preferences.service.ts   un état qui survit à F5
├── composants/
│   ├── boutique.ts              ajoute au panier
│   ├── resume-panier.ts         affiche le panier
│   └── compteur-local.ts        un état local
├── app.ts
└── app.html

docs.title: 5.2.1. A service that contains the state
docs.text:
// =========================================================================
// 20-status-share/src/app/status/panier.service.ts - a ÉTAT PARTAGÉ
// -------------------------------------------------------------------------
// A root service (providedIn: 'root') that contains signals is a
// "store": UN—a single instance for the entire application, which
// all components share. Typical organization:
//    - the ÉTAT: signals PRIVÉS, which can only be modified by the service;
//    - signals in LECTURE SEULE (asReadonly) and computed signals, read by
//      the components;
//    - methods (the “actions”), which are the only ones that can modify the state.
// The service lives as long as the application does: it survives the removal of a
// component... but not a page reload (F5), which restarts
// the application. (No need for additional libraries, such as Pinia
// for Vue.js: services and signals are sufficient.)
// =========================================================================

import { computed, Injectable, signal } from '@angular/core';

export interface Article {
  libelle: string;
  prix: number;
}

@Injectable({ providedIn: 'root' })
export class PanierService {
  private readonly _articles = signal<Article[]>([]);

  readonly articles = this._articles.asReadonly();
  readonly nombre = computed(() => this._articles().length);
  readonly total = computed(() => this._articles().reduce((s, a) => s + a.prix, 0));

  ajouter(article: Article): void {
    this._articles.update((a) => [...a, article]);
  }

  vider(): void {
    this._articles.set([]);
  }
}

A root service containing signals acts as a store ([store]): a single instance, shared by the entire application. It is organized into three parts:

  • line 26: the state, in a private signal: no component can modify it directly;
  • lines 28–30: what the components read: the read-only state ([asReadonly]) and calculated values ([computed]);
  • lines 32–38: the actions, the only methods that can modify the state.

This approach has a key benefit: when a shopping cart is invalid, the only possible modifications occur within the service methods. With [Vue.js], a library ([Pinia]) is typically used for this purpose; with [Angular], services and signals alone suffice.

docs.text:

      }

  protected readonly produits: Article[] = [
    { libelle: 'Consultation', prix: 30 },

}
  • line 17: the component injects the service;
  • line 11: it calls an action.
// 20-etat-partage/src/app/composants/resume-panier.ts - LIT the same shopping cart
import { Component, inject } from '@angular/core';
import { PanierService } from '../etat/panier.service';

@Component({
  selector: 'app-resume-panier',
  template: `
    <div class="card p-3 h-100">
      <h2 class="h6">Panier</h2>
      <p class="mb-2">{{ panier.nombre() }} article(s), {{ panier.total() }} €</p>
      <button class="btn btn-sm btn-outline-danger align-self-start" [disabled]="panier.nombre() === 0"
              (click)="panier.vider()">Vider</button>
    </div>
  `,

  • line 12: it calls another action.

The two components are not aware of each other: there are no inputs or outputs between them. They communicate through the service.

// 20-shared-state/src/app/components/compteur-local.ts - a state LOCAL, which disappears with the component
import { Component, signal } from '@angular/core';

@Component({
  selector: 'app-compteur-local',
  template: `
    <div class="card p-3 h-100">
      <h2 class="h6">État local</h2>
      <button class="btn btn-sm btn-outline-secondary align-self-start" (click)="clics.set(clics() + 1)">{{ clics() }} clic(s)</button>
    </div>
  `,
})
export class CompteurLocal {
  protected readonly clics = signal(0);
}
  • line 14: a local state: each instance of the component has its own counter, which disappears when the instance is destroyed.

docs.title: 5.2.3. A state that survives a page reload
docs.text:
// =========================================================================
// 20-state-sharing/src/app/state/preferences.service.ts - a state that survives F5
// -------------------------------------------------------------------------
// To ensure that data survives a page reload or when the
// the browser, it must be stored DANS in the browser: localStorage (a
// small key-to-string dictionary, unique to each site).
//    - on startup, the service re-reads localStorage;
//    - a function rewrites localStorage with every change.
// No sensitive data (passwords, tokens) is stored there: any script
// on the page can read localStorage.
// =========================================================================

import { effect, Injectable, signal } from '@angular/core';

const CLE = 'exemple20.preferences';

export interface Preferences {
  sombre: boolean;
  taille: number; // text size, in px
}

function lire(): Preferences {
  try {
    return { sombre: false, taille: 16, ...JSON.parse(localStorage.getItem(CLE) ?? '{}') };
  } catch {
    return { sombre: false, taille: 16 }; // unreadable content: default values
  }
}

@Injectable({ providedIn: 'root' })
export class PreferencesService {
  readonly preferences = signal<Preferences>(lire());

  constructor() {
    effect(() => localStorage.setItem(CLE, JSON.stringify(this.preferences())));
  }

   // A preference changes: the object is replaced (the signal detects this)
  modifier(changement: Partial<Preferences>): void {
    this.preferences.update((p) => ({ ...p, ...changement }));
  }
}
  • line 15: the key under which preferences are stored in [localStorage], a small key-to-string dictionary specific to each site;
  • lines 22–28: Upon startup, the saved preferences are read. The default values are supplemented by those that have been saved (using the [...] operator); unreadable content is ignored (line 26);
  • line 32: the preferences, in a signal;
  • line 35: an effect (example 13) rewrites the [localStorage] whenever the signal changes: you don’t have to think about it in every action;
  • lines 39–41: the action that modifies one or more preferences ([Partial<Preferences>]: an object where every property is optional). We replace the object rather than modifying it: a signal only detects changes in value.

Sensitive data (passwords, login tokens) is never stored in the [localStorage]: any script executed by the page can read it. This is why the login token for the [RdvMedecins] application will be stored in a cookie, which is inaccessible to the [JavaScript] code.

docs.title: 5.2.4. The page
docs.text:
// =========================================================================
// 20-etat-partage/src/app/app.ts - three client-side data "scopes"
// -------------------------------------------------------------------------
// Same question as Example 23 from the course NestJS (application scope,
// request, client), transposed to the browser:
//    - the state LOCAL of a component (CompteurLocal) disappears along with it;
//    - the state of a root SERVICE (the shopping cart) is shared by all
//      components and survives their removal—but not F5;
//    - the state stored in localStorage (preferences) survives F5 and
//      browser closing.
// Uncheck and then recheck "Show area," then reload the page: compare.
// =========================================================================

import { Component, inject, signal } from '@angular/core';
import { PreferencesService } from './etat/preferences.service';
import { Boutique } from './composants/boutique';
import { ResumePanier } from './composants/resume-panier';
import { CompteurLocal } from './composants/compteur-local';

@Component({
  selector: 'app-root',
  imports: [Boutique, ResumePanier, CompteurLocal],
  templateUrl: './app.html',
})
export class App {
  protected readonly prefs = inject(PreferencesService);
  protected readonly zoneVisible = signal(true);
}
  • line 27: a local state of the root component: is the field displayed?
@let p = prefs.preferences();
<div class="min-vh-100" [class.bg-dark]="p.sombre" [class.text-light]="p.sombre" [style.font-size.px]="p.taille">
  <div class="container py-4">
    <h1 class="h3 mb-3">Exemple 20 - un état partagé</h1>
    <div class="d-flex flex-wrap gap-4 mb-3">
      <label class="form-check-label">
        <input #dark type="checkbox" class="form-check-input" [checked]="p.sombre"
               (change)="prefs.modifier({ sombre: sombre.checked })"> thème sombre
      </label>
      <label>
        taille du texte
        <input #size type="range" min="12" max="22" [value]="p.taille"
               (input)="prefs.modifier({ taille: +taille.value })"> {{ p.taille }} px
      </label>
      <label class="form-check-label">
        <input #zone type="checkbox" class="form-check-input" [checked]="zoneVisible()"
               (change)="zoneVisible.set(zone.checked)"> afficher la zone
      </label>
    </div>
    @if (zoneVisible()) {
      <div class="row g-3 text-body">
        <div class="col-md-4"><app-boutique /></div>
        <div class="col-md-4"><app-resume-panier /></div>
        <div class="col-md-4"><app-compteur-local /></div>
      </div>
    }
    <p class="mt-3 mb-2">Hors de la zone, un second résumé du MÊME panier (il reste là quand la zone disparaît) :</p>
    <div class="text-body"><app-resume-panier /></div>
  </div>
</div>
  • line 1: [@let] declares a template variable: [p] avoids repeating [prefs.preferences()];
  • Line 2: The preferences apply to the entire page: [[class.bg-dark]] sets the class if the value is true; [[style.font-size.px]] sets a size in pixels;
  • Lines 7–8 and 12–13: Each change triggers the action [modifier];
  • Lines 20–26: The area containing the three components, whether displayed or not;
  • line 28: a second summary of the same shopping cart, outside the area.

[npm start 20-etat-partage]; two items are added to the shopping cart, and the local counter is clicked twice:

You can then verify the three scopes:

  • uncheck and then recheck “show area”: the local counter has reset to 0 (the component was recreated), the shopping cart is intact (the service survived);
  • select the dark theme, then reload the page (F5): the shopping cart is empty (the application has been restarted), the dark theme is retained ([localStorage] has survived).

docs.title: 4.1. Example 17: The Router
docs.text:
A [Angular] application is a single-page application: the browser loads only one page, HTML. However, the [RdvMedecins] application has multiple pages (/login, /calendar, /doctors...), each with its own URL, which can be bookmarked or reloaded. This is the role of the [Angular] router: it associates each URL with a component—the “page”—and displays that component when the URL changes, without making any requests to the server.

17-routeur/src/
├── app/
│   ├── pages/
│   │   ├── accueil.ts
│   │   ├── liste-medecins.ts
│   │   ├── detail-medecin.ts
│   │   ├── recherche.ts
│   │   ├── a-propos.ts
│   │   └── page-introuvable.ts
│   ├── donnees.ts          trois médecins "en dur"
│   ├── app.routes.ts       les routes
│   ├── app.config.ts       la configuration de l'application
│   ├── app.ts
│   └── app.html
├── index.html
└── main.ts

docs.title: 4.1.1. The routes
docs.text:
// =========================================================================
// 17-router/src/app/app.routes.ts - the ROUTES of the application
// -------------------------------------------------------------------------
// An Angular application is a single-page application (SPA: Single
// Page Application): the browser loads only UNE page HTML. When you
// click an internal link, no request is sent to the server: the
// router changes the address displayed by the browser and replaces the
// component displayed in <router-outlet>.
//
// A route associates a CHEMIN with a COMPOSANT (a "page"):
//    'doctors/:id'   :id is a parameter (/doctors/2 -> id = "2");
//    '**            ' any path: the "page not found" page. The
//                     paths are tried in order: it appears as DERNIER.
// title: the title of the browser tab when the page is displayed.
// =========================================================================

import { Routes } from '@angular/router';
import { Accueil } from './pages/accueil';
import { ListeMedecins } from './pages/liste-medecins';
import { DetailMedecin } from './pages/detail-medecin';
import { Recherche } from './pages/recherche';
import { PageIntrouvable } from './pages/page-introuvable';

export const routes: Routes = [
  { path: '', component: Accueil, title: 'Accueil' },
  { path: 'medecins', component: ListeMedecins, title: 'Médecins' },
  { path: 'medecins/:id', component: DetailMedecin, title: 'Un médecin' },
  { path: 'recherche', component: Recherche, title: 'Recherche' },
   // loading DIFFÉRÉ: the code for this page is downloaded only on the
   // first visit (the compiler creates a separate file for it)
  { path: 'a-propos', loadComponent: () => import('./pages/a-propos'), title: 'À propos' },
   // a redirect: the old address leads to the new one
  { path: 'docteurs', redirectTo: 'medecins' },
  { path: '**', component: PageIntrouvable, title: 'Page introuvable' },
];
  • line 24: the routes form an array of objects of type [Routes];
  • line 25: the empty path: the home page, at the address /. A / is never placed at the beginning of a path;
  • line 27: [:id] is a parameter: /doctors/1, /doctors/2... all display the [DetailMedecin] component, which receives the value of [id];
  • line 31: [loadComponent] replaces [component]: the component is loaded only on the first visit to the page. The compiler stores its code in a separate file, which is downloaded at that moment; this speeds up the application’s loading time. We’ll do this for all pages in the case study;
  • line 33: a redirect: /docteurs leads to /medecins;
  • line 34: [**]: any path. Since paths are tried in order, this one is only used if none of the others work: this is the “page not found” page;
  • [title]: the browser tab title when the page is displayed.

docs.title: 4.1.2. Application Configuration
docs.text:
// =========================================================================
// 17-router/src/app/app.config.ts
// -------------------------------------------------------------------------
// provideRouter (routes): the router is added to the application, along with its
// routes (app.routes.ts). withComponentInputBinding(): the parameters
// address parameters (/doctors/:id, ?q=...) are passed to the page components
// as ENTRÉES (input())—see pages/detail-medecin.ts.
// =========================================================================

import { ApplicationConfig } from '@angular/core';
import { provideRouter, withComponentInputBinding } from '@angular/router';
import { routes } from './app.routes';

export const appConfig: ApplicationConfig = {
  providers: [provideRouter(routes, withComponentInputBinding())],
};

Until now, the application configuration was contained in the file [main.ts]. It is now stored separately in [app.config.ts], as in projects created by the command [ng new]:

  • Line 15: [provideRouter] adds the router to the application, along with its routes. [withComponentInputBinding()] passes the address parameters to the page components as entries ([input()], Example 10): this is the simplest way to read them.
// =========================================================================
// 17-router/src/main.ts
// -------------------------------------------------------------------------
// The application’s configuration (its “providers”) is stored separately,
// in app.config.ts: this is the standard structure for an Angular project.
// =========================================================================

import { bootstrapApplication } from '@angular/platform-browser';
import { appConfig } from './app/app.config';
import { App } from './app/app';

bootstrapApplication(App, appConfig).catch((erreur) => console.error(erreur));
  • Line 12: [bootstrapApplication] receives the configuration.
<!doctype html>
<html lang="fr">
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">
  <title>Exemple 17 - le routeur</title>
  <base href="/">
  <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
</head>
<body>
  <app-root></app-root>
</body>
</html>
  • line 6: [<base href="/">]: the address from which the router calculates the paths. Without it, multi-level addresses (/doctors/2) would not work.

docs.title: 4.1.3. The application shell
docs.text:
The root component becomes a shell: it contains elements common to all pages (in this case, the title and links) and a space where the current page is displayed.

// =========================================================================
// 17-router/src/app/app.ts—the application’s “shell”
// -------------------------------------------------------------------------
//    - routerLink="..." : an internal link. In a <a> tag, it produces a
//      valid href, but clicking it does not reload the page: it is the router that
//      takes action. routerLinkActive="active" sets the "active" class (the one from
//      Bootstrap) on the link of the displayed page;
//    - <router-outlet />: the location where the component for the
//      current route is displayed.
// =========================================================================

import { Component, inject } from '@angular/core';
import { toSignal } from '@angular/core/rxjs-interop';
import { NavigationEnd, Router, RouterLink, RouterLinkActive, RouterOutlet } from '@angular/router';
import { filter, map } from 'rxjs';

@Component({
  selector: 'app-root',
  imports: [RouterLink, RouterLinkActive, RouterOutlet],
  templateUrl: './app.html',
})
export class App {
  private readonly router = inject(Router);

   // the current address, in signal form: router.events is a stream
   // (Observable, see Example 19) of navigation events; the
   // end of each navigation, and toSignal turns it into a signal
  protected readonly adresse = toSignal(
    this.router.events.pipe(
      filter((e) => e instanceof NavigationEnd),
       // decodeURIComponent: %C3%A9 becomes active again
      map((e) => decodeURIComponent(e.urlAfterRedirects)),
    ),
    { initialValue: '' },
  );
}
  • line 19: the router directives used by the template;
  • lines 28–35: the current URL, displayed below the links. [router.events] is an observable (a stream of events, as shown in Example 19) that signals each step of the navigation. We retain only the endpoints of navigation (line 30), extract the address from them—including any redirects (line 32)—and [toSignal] transforms the stream into a signal that can be used in the template.

  • Line 5: [routerLink]: an internal link. For a [<a>] tag, it generates a valid [href] attribute (the link can be opened in a new tab), but clicking it does not reload the page: the router is what changes the address and the display. [routerLinkActive="active"] applies the [active] class (derived from [Bootstrap]) to the link on the displayed page. Without the [exact] option, the / link would be active on all pages, since all addresses begin with /;
  • lines 9–10: [[queryParams]]: the parameters placed after the [?] in the URL (/search?q=generalist). The [queryParams: 'ignored'] option keeps the link active regardless of the search;
  • lines 12–13: a link to the redirect, and a link to an address that does not exist;
  • line 17: [<router-outlet />]: the location where the current route component is displayed.

  private readonly router = inject(Router);
  private readonly location = inject(Location);

   // computed: if you navigate from /doctors/1 to /doctors/2, Angular RÉUTILISE
   // the same component and only changes the id property—the computed property updates accordingly
  protected readonly medecin = computed(() => MEDECINS.find((m) => m.id === Number(this.id())) ?? null);

  protected retour(): void {
    this.location.back();

// -------------------------------------------------------------------------
// /search?q=pediatrician: as with the GET form from the NestJS course, the
// page is fully described by its address: you can bookmark it
// bookmark, reload it, or go back. The "q" parameter is also
// as well, as an input to the component.
// =========================================================================

import { Component, computed, inject, input, linkedSignal } from '@angular/core';
import { FormsModule } from '@angular/forms';
import { Router } from '@angular/router';
import { MEDECINS } from '../donnees';

@Component({
  selector: 'app-recherche',
  imports: [FormsModule],
  template: `
    <form class="d-flex gap-2 mb-3" (ngSubmit)="rechercher()">
      <input name="saisie" class="form-control" placeholder="nom ou spécialité" [(ngModel)]="saisie">
      <button class="btn btn-primary">Rechercher</button>
    </form>
    <ul class="mb-0">
      @for (m of resultats(); track m.id) {
        <li>{{ m.prenom }} {{ m.nom }} ({{ m.specialite }})</li>
      } @empty {
        <li class="text-muted">Aucun résultat.</li>
      }
    </ul>
  `,
})
export class Recherche {
  readonly q = input<string>(); // ?q=... (undefined if absent)
  private readonly router = inject(Router);

   // the field starts with the value of URL and updates to it if it changes
   // (Back button), while remaining editable: a linkedSignal
  protected readonly saisie = linkedSignal(() => this.q() ?? '');

  protected readonly resultats = computed(() => {
    const q = (this.q() ?? '').toLowerCase();
    return MEDECINS.filter((m) => `${m.prenom} ${m.nom} ${m.specialite}`.toLowerCase().includes(q));
  });

  protected rechercher(): void {
     // The URL is changed; the display follows the URL (q input)
    this.router.navigate(['/recherche'], { queryParams: { q: this.saisie() } });
  }
}

This page is fully described by its address, just like that of a form GET: you can bookmark it, reload it, or return to it using the Back button.

  • Lines 40–43: The results depend on the address, not on the input: they only change when the form is submitted;
  • line 47: submitting the form changes the address, which changes the [q] entry, which changes the results.
